context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:262:For \(C=A\times B'\), the manuscript explicitly states \(\bar u_0=p\bar v_0\) but excludes a global \(\bar u=p\bar v\), with the class placed in the cross-Hom component; this supports the register's central claim at the level of a stated construction. Its words “en égales ou inégales car” claim both equal and unequal characteristic, broader than the register's mixed-characteristic summary. In the independently opened MP, Example 3.12, p.8, a CM elliptic-curve construction using an order of conductor \(p\) produces nonzero \(p\)-torsion in a specialization cokernel for a product; its ordinary reduction differs from this manuscript's proposed special fibre without a point of order \(p\). The comparison supports a shared failure of integral saturation, not identity of construction or a historical-priority claim.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:289:The notes separately ask for continuity of Picard \(\ell\)-rank, boundedness of Néron–Severi rank, and “Continuité de la torsion de N.S.”, with the instruction to study the possibly “modulaire” Igusa family. CT, 16:21 has a Kummer sequence and an explicitly \(\ell\)-primary torsion comparison, whereas the present special-fibre divisibility defect occurs at the residue characteristic. MP, Proposition 3.6, p.7, gives torsion-freeness of the specialization cokernel after inverting that characteristic, so it leaves room for the phenomenon of E05. No rank calculation here settles torsion continuity or WG H1's nonabelian centralizer hunch.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:391:Oda, Corollary 1.3, pp.69–70/PDF pp.8–9, gives \(\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}=\operatorname{Pic}^0\) for the abelian-scheme situation under its existence hypotheses, a statement about Néron–Severi torsion. It does not assert that a specialization image is saturated, which is the distinct issue of 57:290. The elementary inclusion \(p\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Z\) already separates these notions: both groups are torsion-free, while the cokernel has \(p\)-torsion; this comparison prevents an apparent contradiction between the printed result and the manuscript claim.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:494:**Confidence: medium, because the proposed invariant follows directly from the cross-Hom construction but its relative representability is not supplied:** for a fixed relative class, track the fibres where it lies in \(p\,\operatorname{NS}\), together with the cokernel of the integral Hom specialization map. This separates divisibility of an element from constancy of rank and from torsion-freeness of each fibre, the distinctions made in E04–E08 and D09. CT, 16:21–23 gives a useful comparison for finite versus rational information, but a representability or constructibility theorem for this proposed locus would need a new argument under specified family hypotheses.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:142:RS reports an analytic germ-to-\(\varprojlim\operatorname{Pic}(X_n)\) isomorphism if and only if \(R^1f_*\mathcal O_X\) has finite length, with a source range extending well before this packet. The supplied overlap contains a sufficiency-style *question* under closed-point support at 57:272(ii), not the stated germ map, inverse limit, necessity direction or proof of an iff. Closed-point support is suggestively related to finite length for a coherent module over a noetherian local ring, but that algebraic observation does not recover the missing analytic theorem. The register claim is therefore neither verified nor refuted in full by these scans.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:160:The construction passes from the presheaf quotient to one “exact pour les morphismes fid plats … loc. de type fini,” and then interprets its elements through locally trivial principal homogeneous subobjects. The proposition at 57:276 explicitly assumes existence of the Picard object and faithful flatness of its tau part, while the margin asks “de type fini inutile ?”. CT, 47:3 assumes an abelian scheme and its dual, so this page adds a different representability problem; proving the stated equivalence requires effective descent and the precise quotient category, not just a fibrewise quotient of groups.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:169:After stronger properness, flatness and invariant quasi-projective-cover hypotheses, the author writes “Il semble” that flatness and closedness of \(\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}\) should suffice, followed by “Au concours !”. He immediately wonders whether existence of the full Picard object is indispensable at all. CT, 47:8–9 uses Picard components but does not settle this foundational expectation, and the recurrence of quotient questions on 57:309(b) and 310(9) is evidence that the issue remains a working question within this selection.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:205:The quotient family uses a diagonal finite-group action, and the later argument says “utiliser le fait que c'est un schéma non ramifié” when killing the equivariant group-Hom term. CT, 47:11's contragredient action is a close formal parallel, but does not prove the stronger fixed-part identification under the manuscript's abbreviated “conditions habituelles sur B”. A proof should retain the explicitly added trivial action on \(\operatorname{Pic}_{B/S}^{\tau}\) and verify vanishing as a functor or scheme, since pointwise vanishing alone is not the asserted scheme-level statement.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:262:For \(C=A\times B'\), the manuscript explicitly states \(\bar u_0=p\bar v_0\) but excludes a global \(\bar u=p\bar v\), with the class placed in the cross-Hom component; this supports the register's central claim at the level of a stated construction. Its words “en égales ou inégales car” claim both equal and unequal characteristic, broader than the register's mixed-characteristic summary. In the independently opened MP, Example 3.12, p.8, a CM elliptic-curve construction using an order of conductor \(p\) produces nonzero \(p\)-torsion in a specialization cokernel for a product; its ordinary reduction differs from this manuscript's proposed special fibre without a point of order \(p\). The comparison supports a shared failure of integral saturation, not identity of construction or a historical-priority claim.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:280:The condition \(\operatorname{Im}(u\mu)\subset\operatorname{Im}(v)\), the cup-product obstruction diagram, and the \(\mu_2\)-Picard sequence are concrete ingredients for a deformation calculation. Their doubtful indices, tangent-sheaf readings and partly unlabeled arrows mean that dimensions alone do not verify the intended commutativity or the stated existence implication. CT, 54:3–7 and Oda's remark after Corollary 5.12, p.132/PDF p.71, offer tangent/finite-group-scheme comparators; they supply no identification with the distinct Fourier comparison map at CT, 47:7–8.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:391:Oda, Corollary 1.3, pp.69–70/PDF pp.8–9, gives \(\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}=\operatorname{Pic}^0\) for the abelian-scheme situation under its existence hypotheses, a statement about Néron–Severi torsion. It does not assert that a specialization image is saturated, which is the distinct issue of 57:290. The elementary inclusion \(p\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Z\) already separates these notions: both groups are torsion-free, while the cokernel has \(p\)-torsion; this comparison prevents an apparent contradiction between the printed result and the manuscript claim.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:411:The margin says “à vérifier,” and the body explicitly requires each orbit to lie in an affine open before claiming “c'est facile” and sketching a divisor construction. That obligation belongs to existence and properties of the quotient, beyond the already displayed calculation of global functions. CT, 47:11's transport of an automorphism through a Fourier transform does not provide this quotient-existence step, and no exact completion was found in the supplied context.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:438:Under the family-wise linear equivalence \(x.D-D\sim0\), 57:306 asserts the existence of a “système linéaire borné” containing \(D\), together with a morphism \(X\times P\to P\) realizing the action on divisors. The page supplies neither a construction of the finite-dimensional parameter space nor all the hypotheses needed to interpret the family as a regular action, and the cover's “th. de Chevalley” is not itself a theorem statement. CT, 44:2's Albanese-kernel programme and 44:8's ordinary Picard/Albanese endpoints are comparators, but do not fill this local proof.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:586:The frozen text calls the map from \(\Gamma_S\) to \(B\) an “isom” while describing a translation section of exact order 2. Mathematically the construction needs an embedded constant order-two subgroup, whereas an isomorphism onto the entire positive-dimensional abelian scheme would be a different and impossible assertion in the stated elliptic example. Oda, Corollary 1.3's isogeny-kernel framework helps identify the distinction, but this remains a question about shorthand or reading, not a correction of the source.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:2899:Over \(k=\mathbb F_2\), the finite étale algebra \(R=k^3\) has no single algebra generator: every element has only two possible coordinate values, and its polynomial functions cannot separate all three factors. Nevertheless, after extending scalars to an algebraic closure there are elements with three distinct coordinates, so the Vandermonde discriminant polynomial is not the zero polynomial. Thus passage to the algebraic closure proves polynomial nonvanishing without proving existence of a \(k\)-rational point of its nonvanishing locus. This is a conditional objection to the argument as preserved on this sheet, because an infinitude hypothesis may have been supplied in the antecedent text that is not present here.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:2997:The trace construction uses a complementary module \(\{x:\operatorname{Tr}(xB)\subset A\}\) in a generically étale total quotient algebra, whereas the Kähler construction uses a presentation of differentials; their definitions should not be identified before proving a comparison (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0BW0 and 0BTC, §§49.8–49.9). The page's proposed discrete-valuation comparison therefore calls for an explicit account of finiteness, the generic separability assumption, and the relationship between the trace module and the local complete-intersection presentation. A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:169:After stronger properness, flatness and invariant quasi-projective-cover hypotheses, the author writes “Il semble” that flatness and closedness of \(\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}\) should suffice, followed by “Au concours !”. He immediately wonders whether existence of the full Picard object is indispensable at all. CT, 47:8–9 uses Picard components but does not settle this foundational expectation, and the recurrence of quotient questions on 57:309(b) and 310(9) is evidence that the issue remains a working question within this selection.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:253:The argument seeks finite subgroups distinct generically and coincident specially, then asserts \(u_1\notin p\operatorname{Hom}(A_1,B_1)\) while \(u_0\) is divisible by \(p\). Passing through \(\operatorname{Hom}\otimes\mathbb Q\) identifies the proposed rational map, but membership in the integral Hom group is exactly what fails. CT, 16:21 and 23 likewise preserve finite or integral information before rationalizing, although their prime-to-characteristic cohomological setting is different; unresolved source conditions and the inconsistent-looking inclusion at the start of 57:290 prevent this note from upgrading the sketch to a checked proof.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:336:**Confidence: high, by a direct boundary case:** the asserted equivalence for a fixed finite \(p\)-group \(H\) needs \(H\neq0\), or a quantifier requiring the test for all such groups. For \(H=0\), the tensor map in (i bis) is automatically injective even for the zero map between two nonzero rank-one dual lattices, while (i) fails. Oda, Proposition 3.9, pp.83–84 supplies the nearby duality framework, but this missing qualification is an elementary reading of the current statement, not a correction to its transcription.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:550:The frozen exponent in the pointed-Hom factor is \(\tau\mid0\), while 57:284 inserts a quotient involving \(A'\) beside an expression written for the full relative Picard object. CT, 47:3's dual-abelian-scheme classification suggests that one must check which component is intended, rather than silently identify the full Picard object with its connected dual. This comparison identifies a component/notation question for future image work; it does not select an alternative or add a missing superscript.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:586:The frozen text calls the map from \(\Gamma_S\) to \(B\) an “isom” while describing a translation section of exact order 2. Mathematically the construction needs an embedded constant order-two subgroup, whereas an isomorphism onto the entire positive-dimensional abelian scheme would be a different and impossible assertion in the stated elliptic example. Oda, Corollary 1.3's isogeny-kernel framework helps identify the distinction, but this remains a question about shorthand or reading, not a correction of the source.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3179:Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3185:The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3606:Replace every off-block zero by a sufficiently small positive rational $\varepsilon$, obtaining $C_\varepsilon$, and put $s=\mathbf1^tC_\varepsilon^{-1}\mathbf1$, $C=sC_\varepsilon$, $\xi=C^{-1}\mathbf1$; invertibility, positivity of $s$, and that nonzero minor persist.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:95:CT, 44:4, Theorem 5 proposes a height/intersection identity and a broader fibration statement; CN D12 is a lead concerning its limits. The current Néron–Severi divisibility and extension questions contain no height pairing, pencil intersection formula, sign calculation or vertical correction term. They suggest specialization tests for a later comparison, but do not establish the identity or the proposed reduction in WG H9.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:151:The new quotient is explicitly \(\operatorname{Pic}/\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}\), whereas CT, 16:19 uses \(\operatorname{Pic}(U)/\operatorname{Pic}(U)^0=\operatorname{NS}(U)\) and retains a finite discriminant group. For the same Picard object under the usual identification of \(\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}/\operatorname{Pic}^0\) with Néron–Severi torsion, quotienting by Picard-tau additionally removes that torsion; the two quotients coincide when it vanishes, and the two manuscript situations are not being identified. This distinction matters for the torsion-continuity question on 57:311, while the integral specialization example on 57:289–290 concerns nonsaturation of an image and does not require torsion in either individual Néron–Severi group.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:160:The construction passes from the presheaf quotient to one “exact pour les morphismes fid plats … loc. de type fini,” and then interprets its elements through locally trivial principal homogeneous subobjects. The proposition at 57:276 explicitly assumes existence of the Picard object and faithful flatness of its tau part, while the margin asks “de type fini inutile ?”. CT, 47:3 assumes an abelian scheme and its dual, so this page adds a different representability problem; proving the stated equivalence requires effective descent and the precise quotient category, not just a fibrewise quotient of groups.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:178:The cancellations replace much of “Pol” by “Nér” and replace a torsion condition by equivalence to zero in the descent discussion, while some old notation remains live. Positivity is then imposed separately by “faisceaux inversibles rel! amples” at 57:280 and by the cone at 57:281. This revises the local drafting vocabulary rather than retracting a proved theorem; CT, 47:8–9's Picard/Néron–Severi component calculations are a comparator, not a licence to normalize the surviving mixed notation.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:289:The notes separately ask for continuity of Picard \(\ell\)-rank, boundedness of Néron–Severi rank, and “Continuité de la torsion de N.S.”, with the instruction to study the possibly “modulaire” Igusa family. CT, 16:21 has a Kummer sequence and an explicitly \(\ell\)-primary torsion comparison, whereas the present special-fibre divisibility defect occurs at the residue characteristic. MP, Proposition 3.6, p.7, gives torsion-freeness of the specialization cokernel after inverting that characteristic, so it leaves room for the phenomenon of E05. No rank calculation here settles torsion continuity or WG H1's nonabelian centralizer hunch.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:391:Oda, Corollary 1.3, pp.69–70/PDF pp.8–9, gives \(\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}=\operatorname{Pic}^0\) for the abelian-scheme situation under its existence hypotheses, a statement about Néron–Severi torsion. It does not assert that a specialization image is saturated, which is the distinct issue of 57:290. The elementary inclusion \(p\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Z\) already separates these notions: both groups are torsion-free, while the cokernel has \(p\)-torsion; this comparison prevents an apparent contradiction between the printed result and the manuscript claim.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:791:Tensoring the preceding Kummer sequence is used to identify the rational Tate module of the Brauer group with the orthogonal complement of the Néron–Severi space. context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:2065:Applying the determinant after the transform is proposed to yield a map of relative Picard objects and then maps on components indexed by Néron–Severi sections. The compatibility assertion continues onto the next page. The visible minus sign on the target component is accompanied by a marginal double-negation calculation, signaling that signs are being actively tracked.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:2115:The cohomological formulas are claimed to impose divisibility conditions on powers of the dual Néron–Severi class δ′. The word entier is explained by existence of a cycle with integer coefficients, which is stronger and more specific than mere integrality of a numerical intersection. The visible coefficient discrepancy must be resolved before assessing the exact claimed divisibility.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:2917:Under the finiteness and divisibility hypotheses explicitly imposed on the page, tensoring (8.7) with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) identifies \(V_\ell\operatorname{Br}'(X)\) with the quotient of \(H^2(X,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\) by the image of \(\operatorname{NS}(X)\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell\). context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:151:The new quotient is explicitly \(\operatorname{Pic}/\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}\), whereas CT, 16:19 uses \(\operatorname{Pic}(U)/\operatorname{Pic}(U)^0=\operatorname{NS}(U)\) and retains a finite discriminant group. context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:309:## 4. Torsion modules and the printed Oda comparison

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:345:CT, 54:7 asks whether its Hodge/restricted-Lie extension can be recovered from the group written \(p^A\). Oda, Corollary 5.11, printed p.131/PDF p.70, identifies the Dieudonné module of the full finite group scheme \(A[p]\) with \(H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(A)\), with the Hodge subspace identified by Frobenius/Verschiebung data, over a perfect field of characteristic \(p>0\). This upgrades that precise *printed-paper comparison* beyond CN D05's unreviewed lead, but it does not say that abstract geometric \(p\)-torsion points or a Tate module alone recover the extension. Identifying CT, 54:7's particular restricted-Lie extension with this filtered object still requires checking extension maps, restricted p-operations, Frobenius twists and duality conventions.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:354:Oda, Corollary 5.12, p.131/PDF p.70, associates the relevant Picard \(p\)-torsion Dieudonné data with a canonical subspace of \(H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)\) for smooth proper \(X\) with a rational point over a perfect field of characteristic \(p>0\), rather than asserting the abelian-variety equality without qualification. The following remark, p.132/PDF p.71, relates the dual Dieudonné module of the Picard Frobenius kernel to \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\), including a semilinear twist, and does not append a terminal zero asserting the surjectivity suggested by an overcompressed diagram. This is a useful refinement for the asymmetric Hodge calculations and infinitesimal Picard diagrams of the present package, but not a general Hodge splitting.

hits: context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:262:For \(C=A\times B'\), the manuscript explicitly states \(\bar u_0=p\bar v_0\) but excludes a global \(\bar u=p\bar v\), with the class placed in the cross-Hom component; this supports the register's central claim at the level of a stated construction. Its words “en égales ou inégales car” claim both equal and unequal characteristic, broader than the register's mixed-characteristic summary. In the independently opened MP, Example 3.12, p.8, a CM elliptic-curve construction using an order of conductor \(p\) produces nonzero \(p\)-torsion in a specialization cokernel for a product; its ordinary reduction differs from this manuscript's proposed special fibre without a point of order \(p\). The comparison supports a shared failure of integral saturation, not identity of construction or a historical-priority claim.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:402:The condition \(f_1(t,0)=f_2(1/t,0)\) forces the common Laurent polynomial to be constant, which explains the manuscript's statement that global functions do not separate the points of the glued locus. This gives a concrete obstruction to quasi-affineness, subject to the claimed pushout existing with the stated gluing properties. No exact parallel was found in CT; the nearest divisor/Picard comparisons are CT, 16:19 and 44:8, so this package adds a different kind of example rather than restating those arguments.

hits: context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:77:The Picard, dual abelian scheme and correspondence material relates to CT, 44:8's endpoint examples \(J^1=\operatorname{Pic}^0\) and \(J^n=\operatorname{Alb}^0\). It does not construct CT, 44:2, Theorem 3's abelian variety of algebraically trivial cycles modulo the proposed Albanese relation, or its complementary-degree duality; a universal-property comparison with a modern algebraic representative would require an additional argument. In particular, the current quotient \(\operatorname{Pic}/\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}\), called “non ramifié” on 57:277, has a different numerator, denominator and target from the cycle quotient; CN D08 remains a useful but unreviewed warning about this distinction.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:169:After stronger properness, flatness and invariant quasi-projective-cover hypotheses, the author writes “Il semble” that flatness and closedness of \(\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}\) should suffice, followed by “Au concours !”. He immediately wonders whether existence of the full Picard object is indispensable at all. CT, 47:8–9 uses Picard components but does not settle this foundational expectation, and the recurrence of quotient questions on 57:309(b) and 310(9) is evidence that the issue remains a working question within this selection.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:214:The proposition claims that \(\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}\) is an open subfunctor of finite presentation for proper flat finitely presented \(X/S\), and is also closed with the added projective, geometrically integral hypotheses. Its proof invokes criteria “(viii' b')” and “(viii e)” that are not stated in the supplied 43 scans, so those references are dependencies to locate, not completed arguments to reconstruct from context. CT, 54:6's universal flattening Proposition A concerns a different representing condition, and openness here does not itself establish flatness of the Picard object asked about on 57:310–311.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:354:Oda, Corollary 5.12, p.131/PDF p.70, associates the relevant Picard \(p\)-torsion Dieudonné data with a canonical subspace of \(H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)\) for smooth proper \(X\) with a rational point over a perfect field of characteristic \(p>0\), rather than asserting the abelian-variety equality without qualification. context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:307:The final question asks both extension of \(L_t\) across a trait and algebraic triviality of the special restriction, with a claimed affirmative answer under representability and a broader “Peut-être” for proper flat families with geometrically normal or integral fibres. hits: context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:50:The pointed-Hom product formula on 57:283 and equivariant morphisms into the dual abelian scheme on 57:284 connect directly to CT, 47:3, where a rigidified, fibrewise algebraically trivial product line bundle is classified by a morphism into the dual. The action on \(A'\) “par transport de structure” at 57:284 also matches the contragredient equivariance of CT, 47:11, remark 5. These passages add useful classification and action data, but supply neither an equivariant-kernel descent theorem for the quotient family nor the unit-section check in F01.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:59:CT, 44:2, Theorem 1 characterizes \(N(\xi)\) as the kernel of an Albanese-to-cycle-quotient map, with the qualification “en substance”; CN 44:2:1 treats this as part of the earlier programme. The relative quotient in 57:275–277 and the “système linéaire borné” sought on 57:306 concern divisors and families, but do not define that higher-codimension \(N(\xi)\) or identify its kernel. They are related foundations, not another statement of Theorem 1.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:68:CT, 44:2, Theorem 2 gives a proposed bound by one half of an odd Betti number, and CT, 44:8 proposes a Tate-module realization; CN D09–D10 are unreviewed leads about the scope of such claims. The current Igusa calculation explicitly distinguishes \(\dim H^1(\mathcal O_X)\) from Picard dimension, while 57:291–292 discuss abstract torsion groups. Neither calculation supplies a bound for all parameter-family Albanese quotients, so no second witness of Theorem 2 is established.

A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3191:Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3351:A useful later comparison distinguishes a particular bundle’s integral Chern classes from an integral Fourier transform on the entire Chow group. context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:133:The page asks related questions over a henselian noetherian “bon anneau”: algebraizing Picard images, descending projectivity from completion, and comparing punctured Picard groups near a singularity. Part (ii) imposes \(\operatorname{supp}R^1f_*\mathcal O_X\subset\{y\}\), but the target of its comparison remains the frozen alternative \(\widehat Y\mid\widehat X\), and the margin asks what Mumford's example gives. The completion discussion in CT, 44:3 and CN D07 concerns a different algebraic completion argument; neither it nor CT, 16:19 supplies this analytic/local comparison.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:226:The explicit example has \(\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}_{X/S}\simeq Y'\times {}_2A'\), is called “plat,” and is said not to be “simple” in residue characteristic 2, with \(\dim H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)=\dim A+\dim B\) but \(\dim\operatorname{Pic}=\dim B\). Oda's introduction, printed p.64/PDF p.3, explicitly invokes Igusa in explaining why the reduced Picard variety loses cohomological information, making this a close primary-source comparison. The current example must therefore be distinguished from the *nonflat* examples announced on 57:288: failure of smoothness or reducedness of a fibre is not itself failure of flatness.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:244:“Comme conséquence, on aura des exemples” introduces failure of symmetry, failure of continuity for both Hodge terms, nonflat Picard-tau, and absence of a “bon” abelian subscheme. The previous page states the desired fixed-part behaviour, but this short page does not provide four separately verified families. CT, 47:3–8 assumes abelian schemes and therefore is not contradicted by a proposed extension outside that setting, while WG H2 concerns a nonabelian vanishing-cycle statement that these Picard pathologies do not settle.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:289:The notes separately ask for continuity of Picard \(\ell\)-rank, boundedness of Néron–Severi rank, and “Continuité de la torsion de N.S.”, with the instruction to study the possibly “modulaire” Igusa family. CT, 16:21 has a Kummer sequence and an explicitly \(\ell\)-primary torsion comparison, whereas the present special-fibre divisibility defect occurs at the residue characteristic. MP, Proposition 3.6, p.7, gives torsion-freeness of the specialization cokernel after inverting that characteristic, so it leaves room for the phenomenon of E05. No rank calculation here settles torsion continuity or WG H1's nonabelian centralizer hunch.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:2899:Over \(k=\mathbb F_2\), the finite étale algebra \(R=k^3\) has no single algebra generator: every element has only two possible coordinate values, and its polynomial functions cannot separate all three factors. context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3052:If this is read without further ambient hypotheses, let \(A=k[t]\) and \(B=A\times A/(t)\), with the diagonal \(A\)-algebra structure; then \(B\) is finite and its fibre at every maximal ideal is either \(k(\mathfrak m)\) or \(k(\mathfrak m)\times k(\mathfrak m)\), hence is finite étale. But \(B\simeq A\oplus A/(t)\) as an \(A\)-module is not flat, since multiplication by \(t\) kills a nonzero element, so \(B/A\) is not étale. Accordingly, the proposed equivalence needs the hypotheses of the referenced text to supply flatness or a condition that forces it; the counterexample does not decide whether those hypotheses were already in force. Using a product with the \(A\)-factor ensures that every fibre is nonempty, so this objection is not an artefact of allowing the zero algebra as an empty cover.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3277:The attributed statement is explicitly present in Mumford (1970, §8(vii), p. 76): a nontrivial algebraically trivial line bundle on an abelian variety has vanishing cohomology in every degree. Together with base change, it removes the Poincaré direct image away from the zero section. It does not alone determine the scheme-theoretic structure along that section, the surviving cohomological degree, the determinant twist, or the specific comparison map constructed at the bottom of the page.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3283:**Editorial proof plan:** the direct image of the Poincaré line bundle is perfect, and the zero-section pushforward is perfect because that section is a regular immersion, so the cone of the proposed comparison is perfect. Vanishing of all its derived residue-field fibres then proves that the cone vanishes, by the local perfect-complex criterion (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0DJT and 0G99). The remaining task is to show that the particular map induces the required isomorphisms at the unit, not merely that the two sides have equal cohomology dimensions. **Confidence: high**, because the finite-complex criterion is established and isolates exactly the manuscript’s unfinished step.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3191:Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3197:Under algebraicity of the Künneth components, Jannsen (1992, Corollary 1) identifies the kernel from homological to numerical degree-zero correspondence algebras with the Jacobson radical and proves it nilpotent. This isolates a precise obstruction to obtaining the draft's cohomological semisimplicity from numerical semisimplicity. Nilpotence alone permits a nonzero ideal, so it is not a proof that the two equivalence relations coincide; an additional positivity or equivalence argument must annihilate that kernel. The distinction also prevents treating a numerical projector as a canonical cohomological projector solely because some lift exists.

These results strengthen two particular ingredients appearing in the letters, but the projector statement is published condition \(C\), not the draft's stronger inverse-operator condition \(C_\ell\). context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:2834:Take the ordinary exterior algebra of the free rank-four module with basis \(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2\), and put \(\xi=e_1\wedge f_1+e_2\wedge f_2\); then \(\xi^2=2e_1\wedge f_1\wedge e_2\wedge f_2\), so multiplication by \(\xi^2\) is multiplication by 2 from \(\Lambda^0\) to \(\Lambda^4\), not an integral isomorphism. context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:2899:Over \(k=\mathbb F_2\), the finite étale algebra \(R=k^3\) has no single algebra generator: every element has only two possible coordinate values, and its polynomial functions cannot separate all three factors. Nevertheless, after extending scalars to an algebraic closure there are elements with three distinct coordinates, so the Vandermonde discriminant polynomial is not the zero polynomial. Thus passage to the algebraic closure proves polynomial nonvanishing without proving existence of a \(k\)-rational point of its nonvanishing locus. This is a conditional objection to the argument as preserved on this sheet, because an infinitude hypothesis may have been supplied in the antecedent text that is not present here.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:2997:The trace construction uses a complementary module \(\{x:\operatorname{Tr}(xB)\subset A\}\) in a generically étale total quotient algebra, whereas the Kähler construction uses a presentation of differentials; their definitions should not be identified before proving a comparison (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0BW0 and 0BTC, §§49.8–49.9). The page's proposed discrete-valuation comparison therefore calls for an explicit account of finiteness, the generic separability assumption, and the relationship between the trace module and the local complete-intersection presentation. A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3005:Finite étale covers are indeed invariant under nilpotent thickenings, and the modern statement allows arbitrary thickenings of schemes (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BQB, Lemma 58.8.3). His Lemma 1.2.5 also identifies the Poincaré direct image with the zero-section pushforward of this inverse Hodge line, shifted by \(-g\); this preserves canonicity without choosing a trivialization.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3277:The attributed statement is explicitly present in Mumford (1970, §8(vii), p. 76): a nontrivial algebraically trivial line bundle on an abelian variety has vanishing cohomology in every degree. Together with base change, it removes the Poincaré direct image away from the zero section. It does not alone determine the scheme-theoretic structure along that section, the surviving cohomological degree, the determinant twist, or the specific comparison map constructed at the bottom of the page.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3283:**Editorial proof plan:** the direct image of the Poincaré line bundle is perfect, and the zero-section pushforward is perfect because that section is a regular immersion, so the cone of the proposed comparison is perfect. Vanishing of all its derived residue-field fibres then proves that the cone vanishes, by the local perfect-complex criterion (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0DJT and 0G99). The remaining task is to show that the particular map induces the required isomorphisms at the unit, not merely that the two sides have equal cohomology dimensions. **Confidence: high**, because the finite-complex criterion is established and isolates exactly the manuscript’s unfinished step.

context/MPL_16+47+54+44_notes.md:3351:A useful later comparison distinguishes a particular bundle’s integral Chern classes from an integral Fourier transform on the entire Chow group. Beckmann and de Gaay Fortman (2023, Theorem 3.8) characterize integral lifts of the Poincaré character using a specific one-cycle; under a symmetric ample principal polarization, they also relate this to preservation of Chow groups modulo torsion and to weak integral Fourier transforms. These additional hypotheses and the distinction between rational identities and integral lifts prevent the manuscript’s local heuristic from being treated as a general integral-transform theorem.

hits: context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:429:The exact sequences for \(X'=X\amalg_Y S\) isolate the quotient of units on the finite flat \(Y\) by base units, and the last Picard-type sequence is explicitly qualified by “du moins si” the displayed condition on global units holds. context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:438:Under the family-wise linear equivalence \(x.D-D\sim0\), 57:306 asserts the existence of a “système linéaire borné” containing \(D\), together with a morphism \(X\times P\to P\) realizing the action on divisors. The page supplies neither a construction of the finite-dimensional parameter space nor all the hypotheses needed to interpret the family as a regular action, and the cover's “th. de Chevalley” is not itself a theorem statement. CT, 44:2's Albanese-kernel programme and 44:8's ordinary Picard/Albanese endpoints are comparators, but do not fill this local proof.

context/same_cote_57/MPL_57_271-315_notes.md:512:**Confidence: medium, conditional on the pushout and exact-sequence hypotheses:** take \(X=\mathbb P^1\) and \(Y\) to be two disjoint rational sections, so the unit quotient becomes \(\mathbb G_m^2/\mathbb G_m\simeq\mathbb G_m\). This gives a small test of how a toric term enters a pinched curve's Picard object, explaining why the cover's Chevalley/generalized-Picard theme cannot be treated using abelian varieties alone. CR's warning about finite generation of generalized-Jacobian rational points is a relevant external lead, but the absent cote-149 argument is not re-established here.
